CausalChain: Dietary antioxidants -> Reduction in hepatic ROS and ER stress -> Increased activation of PPARα and suppressed overactivation of PPARγ -> Enhanced fatty acid β-oxidation and reduced lipogenesis in hepatocytes -> Elevated secretion of hepatokines (e.g., FGF21) and favorable lipid mediators -> Improved fatty acid utilization in peripheral tissues and systemic insulin sensitivity
Hypothesis: Mitigating hepatic oxidative stress through dietary antioxidants rebalances PPAR isoform activity—boosting PPARα-mediated catabolism over PPARγ-driven lipogenesis—which in turn enhances endocrine signaling and peripheral lipid utilization, thereby preventing NAFLD progression and improving systemic metabolic health.
Abstract: Emerging evidence indicates that hepatic PPAR isoforms not only govern intrinsic lipid metabolic pathways but also orchestrate inter‐organ communication via endocrine mediators. Building on findings that link PPARα with enhanced fatty acid β-oxidation and PPARγ with adipogenic lipid storage, we propose that modulation of hepatic oxidative stress can recalibrate the balance between these opposing pathways. Specifically, targeted reduction of reactive oxygen species (ROS) via dietary antioxidants may preferentially enhance PPARα activation while concurrently suppressing excess PPARγ activity. This shift is hypothesized to increase the production of beneficial hepatokines such as FGF21 and lipid mediators that promote peripheral fatty acid utilization and systemic insulin sensitivity. Such a mechanism could offer a novel therapeutic strategy to combat non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) and associated metabolic syndromes.
